pos: v.t. (to make longer; to extend in duration)
etymology: From length, Old English lengthu. In the Authorized Version the object lengthened is almost always one of two things: a man's days, which God alone extends, or the cords of a tent that is about to hold more people than it was built for.
biblical_def: Length of days is a gift tied in Scripture to righteousness, and twice to a very concrete righteousness. The law of weights ends with it: “But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee” (Deuteronomy 25:15) — honest scales and long life stand in one sentence. God says the same to Solomon: “And if thou wilt walk in my ways, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as thy father David did walk, then I will lengthen thy days” (1 Kings 3:14). Daniel offers a pagan king the same terms — break off thy sins by righteousness, “if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity” (Daniel 4:27). The other object is a tent: “Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes” (Isaiah 54:2). A barren woman is told to make room, and the lengthening of cords must be matched by the strengthening of stakes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lengthen as to extend in length; to make longer; to elongate; and to protract, as time or duration.
webster_full: LENGTHEN, v.t. To extend in length; to make longer; to elongate.
LENGTHEN, v.t. To protract; to continue in duration; as, to lengthen life.
LENGTHEN, v.i. To grow longer; to extend in length.
PROTRACT, v.t. To draw out or lengthen in time; to continue; to prolong.
ENLARGE, v.t. To make greater in quantity or dimensions; to extend in limits, breadth or size.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 25:15
But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
1 Kings 3:14
And if thou wilt walk in my ways, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as thy father David did walk, then I will lengthen thy days.
Isaiah 54:2
Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes;
Daniel 4:27
Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor; if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity.
corruption_summary: Length of life is pursued as a technical achievement while the moral conditions Scripture attaches to it are ignored, and the church wants Isaiah's lengthened cords without his strengthened stakes.
corruption_paragraphs: An enormous industry now addresses the lengthening of days by diet, medicine and measurement, and Scripture does not despise the care of the body. What it insists on, and what is almost never heard alongside, is the moral condition it repeatedly attaches: just weights, kept commandments, sins broken off by righteousness and mercy shewn to the poor. Deuteronomy 25:15 joins an honest scale to long life in one breath. Whatever else a man does about his years, he is not on the Bible's terms for them while he is keeping two sets of weights.

Isaiah 54:2 carries the more common church error. Growth language is everywhere — enlarge the tent, lengthen the cords, spare not — and the second half of the verse is quietly dropped. Strengthen thy stakes. Cords lengthened over stakes that were never driven deeper do not make a bigger tent; they make a collapse in the first wind. Expansion without deepened doctrine, discipline and eldership is the recurring pattern of ministries that grow fast and fall hard, and the prophet foresaw it in the structure of his own sentence.
roots_summary: Hebrew arak (H748), to be long, to prolong; yowm (H3117), day; meythar (H4340), a tent cord; yathed (H3489), a tent pin or stake.
roots_lines: Hebrew arak (H748) — to be long, to prolong, to lengthen; days lengthened in the land.
Hebrew yowm (H3117) — a day; the measure God lengthens or shortens.
Hebrew meythar (H4340) — a tent cord; what Isaiah tells the barren woman to lengthen.
Hebrew yathed (H3489) — a pin, a stake; what must be strengthened in the same verse.
Hebrew eben shelemah — a perfect stone, a just weight; the condition of Deuteronomy 25:15.
usage: “A perfect and just weight... that thy days may be lengthened” — one sentence.
“Then I will lengthen thy days” — conditioned on walking in God's ways.
“Lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes” — never one without the other.

pos: n. (a tent pin driven into the ground)
etymology: Old English staca, a pin or post. Both occurrences in the Authorized Version are Isaiah's, and both are about a tent: the stakes a growing tent must have strengthened, and the stakes of Zion which shall never be removed.
biblical_def: A stake is what holds a tent to the earth, and Isaiah uses it twice for the security of God's dwelling with his people. The first is a command: “Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes” (Isaiah 54:2). Expansion and anchoring are commanded together, to a woman who had no children and is told to prepare for many. The second is a promise, and it is the stronger of the two: “Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities: thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, neither shall any of the cords thereof be broken” (Isaiah 33:20). The figure is deliberately humble — not a fortress but a tent — and the wonder is that this tent is permanent. Israel had lived in tents that came down every morning. Zion is a tent whose pins stay driven.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a stake as a small piece of wood or timber, sharpened at one end and set in the ground, as for a fence or to support a tent.
webster_full: STAKE, n. A small piece of wood or timber, sharpened at one end and set in the ground, or prepared for setting, as for a fence.
STAKE, n. A stick inserted in the ground to which a beast is fastened, or which supports a tent.
STAKE, n. That which is pledged or wagered; hence, to be at stake, to be in danger or hazard.
TABERNACLE, n. A tent; a temporary habitation; in Scripture, the movable house of God in the wilderness.
HABITATION, n. Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling; place of abode; a settled dwelling.
scriptures: Isaiah 33:20

Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities: thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, neither shall any of the cords thereof be broken.
Isaiah 54:2
Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes;
Isaiah 54:3
For thou shalt break forth on the right hand and on the left; and thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles, and make the desolate cities to be inhabited.
Isaiah 33:21
But there the glorious LORD will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby.
corruption_summary: Permanence is out of fashion — commitments held loosely, memberships provisional, doctrine treated as a stage — where Isaiah promises a tent whose stakes are never removed and commands a growing people to drive theirs deeper.
corruption_paragraphs: The temper of the age prefers everything unstaked: a man keeps his options, a family keeps moving, a believer attends without joining, and doctrine is held as a current position rather than a confession. Isaiah 33:20 sets the opposite picture in the most surprising possible terms. The dwelling is a tabernacle, the most temporary structure a people ever lived in, and the promise is that not one of its stakes shall ever be removed. Permanence is not a property of the material; it is a gift of God to a people he has settled.

Isaiah 54:2 shows what that means for a church in a season of growth. Every stake driven is a decision that limits future movement, and that is precisely its usefulness: elders ordained, members received, a confession subscribed, a building bought, a discipline exercised. These feel like constraints and function as anchors. The recovery is to see that cords can only be lengthened as far as the stakes will hold, and that a people who refuse to drive any stake have not preserved their freedom but their fragility.
roots_summary: Hebrew yathed (H3489), a tent pin or stake; ohel (H168), a tent; meythar (H4340), a cord; naah (H5116) and shaanan (H7600), a quiet habitation.

Hebrew ohel (H168) — a tent, a tabernacle; the humble figure for Zion's permanence.

“Strengthen thy stakes” — the condition of lengthened cords.
“A tabernacle that shall not be taken down” — the humblest figure, the surest promise.

pos: v.t. (to repair; to restore to a sound state)
etymology: Shortened from amend, Latin emendare, to free from fault. The Authorized Version uses it of masons repairing the house of the LORD and of two brothers repairing nets — and the second is the occupation Christ interrupted to make them fishers of men.
biblical_def: Joash's temple restoration puts the word among the trades: the money was given “to such as did the work of the service of the house of the LORD, and hired masons and carpenters to repair the house of the LORD, and also such as wrought iron and brass to mend the house of the LORD” (2 Chronicles 24:12). The house of God required mending, and the workmen were paid to do it. The New Testament use is one of the quietest and most consequential scenes in the gospels: “he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them” (Matthew 4:21; Mark 1:19 records the same). They were not fishing. They were doing the unglamorous maintenance without which the fishing is impossible, and it was in the middle of that work that Christ called them. Scripture's dignity for repair is consistent: the same God who commissions building commissions mending, and calls men off a mended net to mend men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mend as to repair, as anything broken, rent or otherwise injured; to restore to a sound state; to amend.
webster_full: MEND, v.t. To repair, as any thing that is broken, rent, decayed, or otherwise injured; to restore to a sound state.
MEND, v.t. To correct; to set right; to alter for the better; to amend.
MEND, v.i. To grow better; to advance to a better state; to improve.
REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury, dilapidation or partial destruction.
NET, n. An instrument for catching fish and fowls, made with twine or thread interwoven with meshes.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 24:12

And the king and Jehoiada gave it to such as did the work of the service of the house of the LORD, and hired masons and carpenters to repair the house of the LORD, and also such as wrought iron and brass to mend the house of the LORD.
Matthew 4:21
And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them.
Mark 1:19
And when he had gone a little further thence, he saw James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, who also were in the ship mending their nets.
Matthew 4:22
And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him.
corruption_summary: A throwaway economy has lost the habit of repair, and the church has borrowed it — discarding people, marriages and institutions that Scripture would have mended.
corruption_paragraphs: The reflex of the age is replacement. Goods are made not to be mended, and the instinct migrates: a marriage that has torn, an elder who has failed, a congregation that has frayed are set aside for something new rather than repaired. Scripture's bias runs the other way. Joash hired men specifically to mend the house of the LORD rather than to build a different one. Paul tells the Galatians to restore a man overtaken in a fault — the word is the same one used of setting a bone and of mending a net — in the spirit of meekness, considering thyself.

The second recovery is the dignity of maintenance. James and John were mending, not catching, when Christ walked by, and the gospel writers record the detail twice. Most faithful work in a home or a church is of that kind: nothing is being caught, and the nets are being kept fit for the day something is. A man who despises the mending will have nothing to fish with. And the call, when it came, came to men who were found doing the ordinary thing well, in their father's boat, on an ordinary morning.

Hebrew bedeq (H919) — a fissure, a breach; what temple money was collected to close.
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to mend, to fit out, to restore; the nets of Matthew 4:21.

“Mending their nets; and he called them” — called out of maintenance.
“They immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him”.

pos: v.t. (to assemble troops; to number for war)
etymology: Latin monstrare, to show, through Old French mostre, a review of troops. The Authorized Version uses it of the scribe of the host who numbered Judah's soldiers, and once, unforgettably, of the LORD of hosts mustering an army against Babylon.
biblical_def: The office is named twice in the record of Jerusalem's fall, in almost identical words, among the men Nebuzaradan took and slew: “the principal scribe of the host, which mustered the people of the land” (2 Kings 25:19; and again in Jeremiah 52:25). The muster-officer kept the rolls of who could be called out; when the city fell he was executed with the priests and the officers, because a conqueror destroys the machinery of resistance first. The theological use is Isaiah's, and it stands the whole idea on its head: “The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people; a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the LORD of hosts mustereth the host of the battle” (Isaiah 13:4). The army being mustered is a coalition of pagan kingdoms, and the officer calling the roll is God. The nations think they are assembling for their own ends; Isaiah tells the reader whose muster it actually is.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines muster as to collect troops for review, parade, exercise or service; to assemble or bring together.
webster_full: MUSTER, v.t. To collect troops for review, parade, exercise, or for other purposes.
MUSTER, v.t. To assemble or bring together; as, to muster all one's strength.
MUSTER, n. An assembling of troops for review, or a review itself; a register or roll of troops mustered.
HOST, n. An army; a number of men embodied for war; and in Scripture, the armies of heaven.
REVIEW, n. A survey; a re-examination; and in military affairs, an inspection of troops under arms.
scriptures: 2 Kings 25:19

And out of the city he took an officer that was set over the men of war, and five men of them that were in the king's presence, which were found in the city, and the principal scribe of the host, which mustered the people of the land, and threescore men of the people of the land that were found in the city:
Jeremiah 52:25

He took also out of the city an eunuch, which had the charge of the men of war; and seven men of them that were near the king's person, which were found in the city; and the principal scribe of the host, who mustered the people of the land; and threescore men of the people of the land, that were found in the midst of the city.
Isaiah 13:4
The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people; a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the LORD of hosts mustereth the host of the battle.
Isaiah 13:5
They come from a far country, from the end of heaven, even the LORD, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land.
corruption_summary: History is read as the sum of human agency, with nations mustering their own armies for their own reasons, where Isaiah puts God himself at the head of the muster-roll of the kingdoms.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard account of great events is exhaustively secondary: interests, resources, ideologies and personalities, and no room at any point for a governing hand. Isaiah 13:4 does not deny a single one of those factors — the noise is real, the kingdoms are really gathered, the tumult is genuine — and then it names the officer: the LORD of hosts mustereth the host of the battle. The Medes who took Babylon had their own motives and served God's purpose without consulting him about it. This is the doctrine of providence at its least comfortable and most necessary, and Scripture asserts it precisely where the armies are pagan.

The other use supplies the sober human note. The principal scribe who mustered the people of the land died with the rest when the city fell. Records, rolls, preparations and officers are real and worth keeping — Scripture never counsels fatalism — and they do not finally save a people under judgment. The principle to recover is the one Israel kept forgetting: an horse is a vain thing for safety, and the muster that decides an outcome is the LORD's.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaba (H6633), to wage war, to muster; paqad (H6485), to number or appoint; caphar (H5608), to count, hence the scribe; tsaba (H6635), a host or army.

“The LORD of hosts mustereth the host of the battle” — whose muster it is.
“A tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together”.

pos: v.t. (to put in order; to dress; to adjust)
etymology: Old English trymman, to strengthen or set in order. The Authorized Version uses it three times, and the range is remarkable: a beard left untrimmed in loyalty, a nation trimming its way to seek love, and ten virgins trimming their lamps at midnight.
biblical_def: Mephibosheth's untrimmed beard is a legal argument. When David returned, Mephibosheth “had neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace” (2 Samuel 19:24) — his body was the evidence that he had not celebrated the king's exile. Jeremiah uses the verb for a very different grooming: “Why trimmest thou thy way to seek love? therefore hast thou also taught the wicked ones thy ways” (Jeremiah 2:33). Judah dressed up her conduct to attract lovers, and became so skilled at it that she instructed the wicked. The third use is the parable: “Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps” (Matthew 25:7). All ten trimmed; the trimming was not the difference. Five had oil and five had none, and the lamps of the foolish went out precisely when they were finally attended to. Preparation that begins at the cry is too late.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines trim as to make right; to put in due order; to dress; to decorate; and, of a lamp, to snuff or clean for burning.
webster_full: TRIM, v.t. To make right, neat or pleasing; to adjust; to put in due order the parts of a thing.
TRIM, v.t. To dress; to decorate; to invest or embellish with extra ornaments.
TRIM, v.t. To make trim; as, to trim a lamp, that is, to snuff or clean the wick.
TRIM, v.i. To balance; to fluctuate between parties, so as to appear to favor each.
LAMP, n. A vessel with a wick, used for the combustion of oil or other inflammable substance, for the purpose of producing light.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 19:24

And Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king, and had neither dressed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace.
Jeremiah 2:33
Why trimmest thou thy way to seek love? therefore hast thou also taught the wicked ones thy ways.
Matthew 25:7
Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.
Matthew 25:8
And the foolish said unto the wise, Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out.
corruption_summary: Presentation has become the main labour of religion — ways trimmed to be found attractive — while the parable warns that every lamp can be trimmed at midnight and only the ones with oil keep burning.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 2:33 names a temptation the church has never outgrown: trimming the way to seek love. The verb is about grooming conduct for an audience, making the path look attractive to the ones whose favour is wanted, and the prophet adds the sting — a people who become expert at it end up teaching the wicked ones their ways. A ministry that arranges its doctrine, its language and its emphases by what will be well received has not merely compromised; it has become an instructor in compromise for anyone watching.

Matthew 25 exposes the deeper danger, which is that trimming is indistinguishable from readiness right up to the moment it matters. All ten virgins slept, all ten woke, all ten trimmed their lamps, and the trimming of the foolish is what revealed that they had no oil. Outward preparation performed at the last hour cannot supply what was never there. And 2 Samuel 19 shows the opposite and rarer thing: a man who did not trim at all for weeks, whose neglected beard was his evidence of loyalty to an absent king.

roots_lines: Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do, to make, to dress; Mephibosheth had not dressed his feet.
Hebrew yatab (H3190) — to make good, to make fair; why trimmest thou thy way.
Greek kosmeo (G2885) — to arrange, to put in order, to adorn; the virgins trimmed their lamps.
Greek lampas (G2985) — a torch, a lamp; what all ten possessed and only five could keep lit.
Greek elaion (G1637) — oil; the one thing trimming could not supply.
usage: “Nor trimmed his beard... until the day he came again in peace” — loyalty visible.
“Why trimmest thou thy way to seek love?” — conduct groomed for an audience.
“Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps” — all ten did.

pos: v.t. (to lay with stone or brick; to floor)
etymology: Latin pavire, to beat or ram down. The Authorized Version uses the participle twice, and both are extraordinary: the sapphire pavement under the feet of the God of Israel, and a chariot paved with love.
biblical_def: On the mountain, seventy elders with Moses and Aaron were given a sight Scripture reports with great restraint: “And they saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness” (Exodus 24:10). The description stops at his feet. What is recorded is the floor — blue, clear as the heavens, and paved, which is to say laid deliberately — and the narrative notes that upon the nobles of Israel he laid not his hand, and they did eat and drink. The other use turns the same craft toward affection: of Solomon's chariot, “He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the covering of it of purple, the midst thereof being paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song of Solomon 3:10). Silver, gold and purple are inventoried, and then the material of the midst is named as love. What a thing is floored with is what it rests on.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pave as to lay or cover with stone or brick, so as to make a level or convenient surface for carriages or foot passengers.
webster_full: PAVE, v.t. To lay or cover with stone or brick, so as to make a level or convenient surface.
PAVE, v.t. To prepare a passage; to facilitate the introduction of; as, to pave the way.
PAVEMENT, n. A floor or covering consisting of stones or bricks, laid and fitted for a passage.
SAPPHIRE, n. A precious stone of a blue color, of various shades, next in hardness to the diamond.
CLEARNESS, n. Freedom from obscurity; brightness; transparency; as, the clearness of the sky.
scriptures: Exodus 24:10
And they saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness.
Song of Solomon 3:10
He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the covering of it of purple, the midst thereof being paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.
Exodus 24:11
And upon the nobles of the children of Israel he laid not his hand: also they saw God, and did eat and drink.
Ezekiel 1:26

And above the firmament that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone: and upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man above upon it.
corruption_summary: Familiarity with God is now assumed as a starting point, where Exodus 24 records elders who saw him and reports only the pavement under his feet, and notes with relief that he laid not his hand upon them.
corruption_paragraphs: Much contemporary devotion begins where Exodus 24 declines to go. God is addressed with an easy intimacy, described confidently, and approached as though nearness were the natural human condition rather than a mercy. The text is a lesson in reverent reticence: they saw the God of Israel, and then the inspired writer turns his eye downward and tells us about the floor. Sapphire, clear as the body of heaven, paved. Ezekiel does the same, with a sapphire throne above the firmament and a likeness as the appearance of a man upon it, and then moves at once to the appearance of the brightness round about.

The verse that follows is the one to preach beside it: and upon the nobles of the children of Israel he laid not his hand: also they saw God, and did eat and drink. That the elders survived is treated as the remarkable thing, and then they ate a covenant meal in his presence. Reverence and communion are not rivals; the second is safe only because of the first. The principle to recover is that the God who is truly approachable in Christ is the God under whose feet is a pavement like heaven for clearness, and that both facts belong in the same worship.
roots_summary: Hebrew libnah (H3840), a pavement or transparency; cappiyr (H5601), sapphire; ratsaph (H7528), to pave or tessellate; ahabah (H160), love.
roots_lines: Hebrew libnah (H3840) — a pavement, a whiteness or transparency; under the feet of the God of Israel.
Hebrew cappiyr (H5601) — sapphire; the stone of the pavement and of Ezekiel's throne.
Hebrew ratsaph (H7528) — to lay with stones, to pave; the midst paved with love.
Hebrew ahabah (H160) — love; the material named where a material was expected.
Hebrew etsem hashamayim — the body of heaven; the clearness the pavement is likened to.

“Upon the nobles... he laid not his hand” — the mercy in the next verse.
“The midst thereof being paved with love” — what the chariot rests on.

pos: n. (a heap, especially of wood for burning)
etymology: Latin pila, a pillar or pier. The Authorized Version uses the noun twice, and in both it means a pyre — the heaped wood of a burning, in Isaiah for Tophet and in Ezekiel for the bloody city.
biblical_def: Isaiah ends his oracle against Assyria with the furnace prepared for its king: “For Tophet is ordained of old; yea, for the king it is prepared; he hath made it deep and large: the pile thereof is fire and much wood; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of brimstone, doth kindle it” (Isaiah 30:33). Tophet was the valley where Israel had burned its own children to Molech; the prophet turns the place of Judah's worst sin into the figure of God's judgment on the tyrant. Two details govern the verse: the pile was ordained of old, prepared long before the king who would need it, and it is kindled not by human hands but by the breath of the LORD. Ezekiel uses the same image against Jerusalem herself: “Woe to the bloody city! I will even make the pile for fire great” (Ezekiel 24:9). God builds no pile for an enemy he will not also build for a guilty city bearing his own name.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pile as a heap; a mass or collection of things thrown together in a heap; and specifically, a heap of combustibles for burning a body.
webster_full: PILE, n. A heap; a mass or collection of things in a roundish or elevated form.
PILE, n. A collection of combustibles for burning a dead body; a funeral pile.
PILE, n. A large stake or piece of timber, pointed and driven into the earth, as for the support of a building.
TOPHET, n. In Scripture, a place near Jerusalem in the valley of Hinnom, where children were sacrificed to Moloch.
BRIMSTONE, n. Sulphur; a hard, brittle, inflammable substance, of a lemon yellow color.
scriptures: Isaiah 30:33

For Tophet is ordained of old; yea, for the king it is prepared; he hath made it deep and large: the pile thereof is fire and much wood; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of brimstone, doth kindle it.
Ezekiel 24:9
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Woe to the bloody city! I will even make the pile for fire great.
Isaiah 30:27
Behold, the name of the LORD cometh from far, burning with his anger, and the burden thereof is heavy: his lips are full of indignation, and his tongue as a devouring fire:
Ezekiel 24:6
Wherefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose scum is therein, and whose scum is not gone out of it! bring it out piece by piece; let no lot fall upon it.
corruption_summary: Divine judgment is widely treated as sub-Christian and unworthy of God, where the prophets describe a pile ordained of old and kindled by God's own breath, and aim the same fire at Jerusalem as at Assyria.
corruption_paragraphs: It is now common to hear that the wrath in passages like Isaiah 30:33 belongs to a primitive stratum of religion which the gospel has outgrown, and that a God of love could not be described kindling a pyre. Two features of the text make that reading impossible. First, the pile is ordained of old — not an outburst of temper but a settled purpose, older than the offender. Second, Ezekiel aims the identical image at Jerusalem, the city of God's own covenant, and calls her the bloody city. A judgment that falls hardest on the household of God is not tribal favouritism; it is holiness, and the New Testament says judgment must begin at the house of God.

The place Isaiah chose carries the argument further. Tophet was where Judah had burned her sons and daughters in the fire to Molech, and God takes the scene of the nation's deepest abomination as the figure of his own righteous burning. The principle to recover is that God's wrath is not the opposite of his love but its defence: a God who would not prepare a pile for tyrants and for bloody cities is a God indifferent to the children in the valley. And the gospel does not remove the fire; it tells us who bore it.
roots_summary: Hebrew medurah (H4071), a pile or pyre; Topheth (H8613), Tophet; gophriyth (H1614), brimstone; neshamah (H5397), breath.
roots_lines: Hebrew medurah (H4071) — a pile of fuel, a pyre; the pile of Isaiah 30:33 and Ezekiel 24:9.
Hebrew Topheth (H8613) — Tophet, the place of burning in the valley of Hinnom.
Hebrew gophriyth (H1614) — brimstone, sulphur; the stream that kindles the pile.
Hebrew neshamah (H5397) — breath; the breath of the LORD doth kindle it.
Hebrew ir haddamim — the city of bloods; Ezekiel's name for Jerusalem under judgment.
usage: “Tophet is ordained of old” — a settled purpose, not a temper.
“The breath of the LORD... doth kindle it” — no human hand.
“Woe to the bloody city! I will even make the pile for fire great”.

etymology: Old English sceap, form or created thing, from scieppan, to create. The Authorized Version uses the noun three times, and they set an important boundary: the Spirit descended in a bodily shape, the Father's shape no man has seen, and the locusts of the fifth trumpet had shapes like horses.
biblical_def: At the Jordan “the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased” (Luke 3:22). Luke is careful: a bodily shape, visible, and like a dove rather than simply a dove. Against that stands our Lord's word to men who claimed God as their authority: “And the Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me. Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape” (John 5:37). The Father has no shape that men have seen, and the second commandment rests on that fact. The third use is apocalyptic and deliberately monstrous: “And the shapes of the locusts were like unto horses prepared unto battle; and on their heads were as it were crowns like gold, and their faces were as the faces of men” (Revelation 9:7). Scripture permits God to give a visible shape when he chooses, and forbids men to assign him one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shape as form or figure; external appearance; the form or figure of a thing as it strikes the eye.
webster_full: SHAPE, n. Form or figure; external appearance; that which constitutes a particular form.
SHAPE, n. The form of the body; make; as, a person of elegant shape.
SHAPE, v.t. To form or create; to mould or make into a particular form.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance.
SIMILITUDE, n. Likeness; resemblance; likeness in nature, qualities or appearance.
scriptures: Luke 3:22
And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased.
John 5:37
And the Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me. Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape.
Revelation 9:7
And the shapes of the locusts were like unto horses prepared unto battle; and on their heads were as it were crowns like gold, and their faces were as the faces of men.
Deuteronomy 4:15
Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire:
corruption_summary: God is routinely pictured, imagined and depicted to suit the imaginer, when Christ says plainly that no man has seen the Father's shape and Deuteronomy grounds the second commandment on exactly that.
corruption_paragraphs: Images of God are everywhere — in art, in film, in the private imagination cultivated as a devotional practice — and the usual defence is that they are aids rather than idols. Deuteronomy 4:15 anticipates the defence and forecloses it: Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire. The prohibition is not arbitrary; it rests on a fact about the event. They heard a voice and saw no shape, and therefore any shape they made would be a lie about him. Our Lord states the same fact in John 5:37 to men who were sure they knew the Father.

The other side is equally important and is where the Reformed confessions have always been careful. God has given visible signs when he pleased — a bodily shape like a dove at the Jordan, the fire, the cloud — and supremely he has given his Son, who is the image of the invisible God and the express image of his person. The answer to the hunger for a visible God is not a picture we make but a Christ we are given. He that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and the church has the sacraments God appointed rather than the images men invent.
roots_summary: Greek eidos (G1491), outward appearance, shape; homoioma (G3667), a likeness; Hebrew temunah (H8544), a similitude or form; pesel (H6459), a graven image.
roots_lines: Greek eidos (G1491) — that which is seen, outward appearance; bodily shape in Luke 3:22.
Greek eidos (G1491) — the same word Christ uses: nor seen his shape, John 5:37.
Greek homoioma (G3667) — a likeness, a resemblance; the shapes of the locusts.
Hebrew temunah (H8544) — a likeness, a similitude; ye saw no manner of similitude.
Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image; what the second commandment forbids making.
usage: “The Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove” — a sign God gave.
“Nor seen his shape” — and therefore no man may assign him one.
“Ye saw no manner of similitude” — the ground of the second commandment.

pos: n. (one who plays on a musical instrument)
etymology: From play, Old English plegian. In the Authorized Version a player is never an actor or a gamester but a musician, and the word appears at two of the most consequential musical moments in Scripture.
biblical_def: Saul's servants propose a remedy that brings David to court: “Let our lord now command thy servants, which are before thee, to seek out a man, who is a cunning player on an harp: and it shall come to pass, when the evil spirit from God is upon thee, that he shall play with his hand, and thou shalt be well” (1 Samuel 16:16). The search for a skilful player is the providence that carries the anointed shepherd into the king's house. The other uses are liturgical. In the procession psalm, “The singers went before, the players on instruments followed after; among them were the damsels playing with timbrels” (Psalm 68:25) — an ordered company with voice leading and instruments behind. And in the psalm of Zion's citizenship the players are placed in the city itself: “As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there: all my springs are in thee” (Psalm 87:7). Skill with an instrument is treated throughout as a real gift, sought out, employed, and set in the worship of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a player as one who plays; a musician; one who plays on an instrument of music; also, an actor on the stage.
webster_full: PLAYER, n. One who plays in any game or sport.
PLAYER, n. A musician; as, a player on the lute or on the harp.
PLAYER, n. An actor of dramatic scenes; one whose occupation is to imitate characters on the stage.
CUNNING, a. Knowing; skilful; experienced; well-instructed; as, a cunning workman.
PSALTERY, n. An instrument of music used by the Hebrews, the form of which is not now known.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 16:16

Let our lord now command thy servants, which are before thee, to seek out a man, who is a cunning player on an harp: and it shall come to pass, when the evil spirit from God is upon thee, that he shall play with his hand, and thou shalt be well.
Psalm 68:25
The singers went before, the players on instruments followed after; among them were the damsels playing with timbrels.
Psalm 87:7
As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there: all my springs are in thee.
1 Samuel 16:23
And it came to pass, when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.
corruption_summary: Musical skill in worship is treated either as performance to be admired or as a worldly intrusion to be resisted; Scripture sought out a cunning player, set players in the temple procession, and put them in Zion.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite mistakes crowd the subject. The first turns the player into a performer: the platform is a stage, excellence is applauded for itself, and the congregation becomes an audience. The second, in reaction, treats skill as suspect and prefers incompetence as though it were humility. Scripture supports neither. Saul's servants were told to seek out a cunning player, and God used that search to bring David into the king's house. The chronicler records instructors in song, men instructed and cunning, numbered and appointed. Skill is sought, trained and honoured.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the ordering in Psalm 68:25: the singers went before, and the players on instruments followed after. The voice of the congregation leads and the instruments support; when that order reverses, the people stop singing and start listening. And Psalm 87:7 gives the final dignity of the office — the players on instruments are not visitors to Zion but citizens of it, with all their springs in her. Music in the worship of God is not a concession to weakness but part of the city's permanent life.
roots_summary: Hebrew nagan (H5059), to play a stringed instrument; kinnowr (H3658), a harp; shiyr (H7891), to sing; chalal (H2490), to play the pipe.
roots_lines: Hebrew nagan (H5059) — to strike the strings, to play; the cunning player of 1 Samuel 16:16.
Hebrew kinnowr (H3658) — a harp or lyre; David's instrument before Saul.
Hebrew shiyr (H7891) — to sing; the singers who went before the players.
Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to bore, to play the pipe; the players of Psalm 87:7.
Hebrew maayan (H4599) — a spring, a fountain; all my springs are in thee.
usage: “Seek out a man, who is a cunning player on an harp” — skill sought deliberately.
“The singers went before, the players on instruments followed after” — the order.
“As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there” — citizens of Zion.

pos: v.t. (to manage; to dispense, as a trust)
etymology: Latin administrare, to serve or manage, from ad and ministrare, to minister. The Authorized Version uses the passive twice, both in the same chapter, and both about the handling of other people's money for the poor.
biblical_def: Paul is gathering a large collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, and he takes extraordinary care about who handles it. A brother is sent with Titus, “who was also chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace, which is administered by us to the glory of the same Lord, and declaration of your ready mind” (2 Corinthians 8:19). Then he states his reason with unusual bluntness: “Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us” (2 Corinthians 8:20), and adds in the next verse that he provides for honest things not only in the sight of the Lord but in the sight of men. The money was not entrusted to one man, however apostolic. It travelled with a delegate chosen of the churches, so that the administration could be seen as well as done. Administration in the New Testament is a spiritual office with an accountant's discipline.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines administer as to act as minister or chief agent in managing public affairs; to dispense, as justice or a sacrament; to afford, to supply.
webster_full: ADMINISTER, v.t. To act as minister or chief agent in managing public affairs, under laws or a constitution.
ADMINISTER, v.t. To dispense; as, to administer justice or the sacrament.
ADMINISTER, v.t. To afford, give or furnish; as, to administer relief or comfort.
STEWARD, n. A man employed to manage the domestic concerns of a family; one who is entrusted with the property of another.
ACCOUNTABLE, a. Liable to be called to account; answerable to a superior; responsible.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 8:19
And not that only, but who was also chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace, which is administered by us to the glory of the same Lord, and declaration of your ready mind:
2 Corinthians 8:20
Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us:
2 Corinthians 8:21
Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.
1 Corinthians 4:2
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
corruption_summary: Ministries routinely ask to be trusted rather than audited, treating scrutiny of money as an insult to spiritual men; Paul built his collection so that no man could blame him, and said so in writing.
corruption_paragraphs: A familiar pattern in religious fund-raising is the appeal to trust: the work is God's, the leaders are godly, and to ask hard questions about the handling of funds is treated as carnal suspicion. 2 Corinthians 8:20 is the apostolic refutation, written by a man who had every claim to be trusted on sight. He would not carry the money alone. He accepted a delegate chosen by the churches, and he stated the motive plainly — avoiding this, that no man should blame us. Paul did not merely intend to be honest; he arranged matters so that his honesty could be verified by people who did not know him.

Verse 21 gives the principle in full: providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men. Both halves are required. A man who satisfies only the second becomes a hypocrite; a man who appeals only to the first becomes unaccountable, and the history of the church is littered with the wreckage. Add to it the requirement of 1 Corinthians 4:2 — it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful — and the shape of Christian administration is clear: plural handling, open books, and delegates the churches themselves chose.
roots_summary: Greek diakoneo (G1247), to serve, to minister; diakonia (G1248), a ministry or service; charis (G5485), grace, here the collection itself; oikonomos (G3623), a steward.
roots_lines: Greek diakoneo (G1247) — to serve, to administer; the verb of 2 Corinthians 8:19-20.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — service, ministry; Paul's word for the relief collection itself.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace; the gift is called a grace administered to God's glory.
Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint by show of hands; the brother chosen of the churches.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a house-manager, a steward; required to be found faithful.
usage: “Chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace” — plural handling.
“That no man should blame us in this abundance” — the stated motive.
“Not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” — both.
